(CNN)  -- Clashes between Somalia's transitional government and the Al-Shabab militia left 103 people dead and 420 others wounded, Somali officials said Friday. The fighting in Mogadishu between the rebel group and the government has raged for nine days. The fighting in Mogadishu between the rebel group and the government has raged for nine days, said Farhan Ali Mohamud, information minister of the Somali government. Human rights groups deplored the high number of casualties, urging both sides to comply with international law in respect to the civilian population. Thousands of families have fled the capital, Mogadishu, seeking a safer environment in camps south of the city. "The people of Somalia have once again been subjected to unbearable violence," said Pascal Mauchle, head of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Somalia. "The daily struggle for survival is exhausting their capacity to cope." Humanitarian groups expressed concern, too, that Somalis will not have access to medical care. The international medical agency Doctors Without Borders said it was forced to close an outpatient clinic in Mogadishu to ensure safety for its staff. "With so few medical facilities available in Somalia, it is crucial that people are able to access those that are still functioning," said Alfonso Laguna, head of the agency in the region. The new round of fighting stems from an interpretation of sharia law, or Islamic law, the spokesman said. Somalia's new President Sheikh Sharif Ahmed has recently approved implementing sharia law, but the rebel group wants the country to institute a stricter form. A spokesman for the rebel group said it has recruited many fighters for the battle against the government. "It is not only Somali jihadists that are fighting in Mogadishu against the government. There are also foreign Muslim jihadist brothers who are fighting side by side with us," said Sheikh Hassan Ya'qub, a spokesman for al-Shabaab. Abdiraman Abdi Shakur Warsame, minister of international cooperation for Somalia's transitional government, issued a stern warning to the rebels in an address to a young audience celebrating Somali youth day at the capital. "The government is determined to defend itself from these religious gangs who are covering in the name of Islam and I assure you that in the course of coming days, we will eliminate these elements and some of them will be forced out of the country," Warsame said. The U.S. Embassy in Kenya released a statement about the fighting. "The extremists who are instigating these attacks have no regard for the well-being of Somalis and are undermining the peaceful efforts of the legitimate government to further national reconciliation," the statement said. "The United States is particularly disturbed at reports that foreign fighters and those who rejected dialogue in 2006 are participating in this effort to forcibly remove a legitimate Somali government from power." Journalist Mohamed Amiin Adow contributed to this report.

A representative of the militia stated that it had brought on many combatants to fight against the government. "Somali jihadists aren't the only ones battling the government in Mogadishu. Foreign Muslim jihadist brothers are also standing shoulder to shoulder with us in this fight," said Sheikh Hassan Ya'qub, an al-Shabaab spokesman.

Abdiraman Abdi Shakur Warsame, who serves as minister of international cooperation for the transitional government, delivered a forceful warning to the rebels while speaking to a youthful crowd marking Somali youth day in the capital. "This government is committed to protecting itself against these religious gangs who hide behind the name of Islam, and I promise you that in the days ahead, we will wipe out these forces, and some will be driven out of the nation," Warsame declared.

The United States Embassy in Kenya put out a statement regarding the violence. "Those extremists behind these attacks care nothing for the welfare of Somalis and are working against the peaceful attempts by the rightful government to advance national reconciliation," the statement read. # Escalating Violence in Mogadishu Deepens Somalia's Humanitarian Crisis

Nine days of intense fighting between Somalia's transitional government forces and the Al-Shabab militia have turned parts of Mogadishu into a battleground, leaving at least 103 people dead and 420 others wounded, according to Somali officials. The clashes represent one of the deadliest episodes of urban warfare the capital has witnessed in recent months, underscoring the fragile state of security in the war-torn nation.

At the heart of the conflict lies a dispute over the implementation of sharia law. While both sides claim to support Islamic governance, they remain deeply divided over how strictly it should be applied. Al-Shabab, an extremist group seeking to impose a far more rigid interpretation of religious law, has repeatedly challenged the transitional government's authority, rejecting its more moderate approach. These ideological differences have fueled the violence, transforming a political and religious disagreement into a bloody armed struggle.

The human cost of the fighting has been staggering. As gunfire and shelling echoed through residential neighborhoods, thousands of families were forced to abandon their homes, joining the ranks of the displaced in a country already grappling with widespread instability. Streets that once bustled with daily life emptied as civilians fled in search of safety, carrying whatever belongings they could gather.

Compounding the crisis, the escalating violence has crippled the region's already limited healthcare infrastructure. Humanitarian organizations, including Doctors Without Borders, were forced to close medical facilities amid the dangerous conditions, cutting off access to essential care for countless people. In a country where functioning hospitals and clinics are scarce, the closure of these facilities has proven devastating. The wounded have struggled to receive treatment, and those with chronic conditions or urgent medical needs have found themselves with few, if any, options.

The combination of mounting casualties, mass displacement, and the collapse of medical services has pushed an already dire humanitarian situation to the brink. For the civilians of Mogadishu, caught between warring factions, the past nine days have brought immeasurable suffering—and with no clear resolution in sight, the future remains uncertain.

At least 45 people have been killed and more than 120 wounded in the clashes, according to hospital officials and local authorities. The dead include government soldiers, militia fighters, and an unknown number of civilians caught in the crossfire.

## Humanitarian Crisis Deepens

"Our forces are determined to protect the population and defeat those who seek to destabilize our nation," a government spokesperson told reporters. "We will not allow extremists to hold this city hostage."

Analysts note that control of Mogadishu remains fiercely contested, with the government relying heavily on support from allied forces to hold strategic positions.

"The situation in the capital remains volatile," said one regional security analyst. "Without a sustained political solution alongside security operations, we risk seeing these cycles of violence repeat."

**MOGADISHU, Somalia** — At least 43 people were killed and more than 120 wounded over the weekend as clashes erupted between government forces and militant fighters across several districts of the Somali capital, according to hospital officials and aid workers.

The fighting, some of the most intense in recent months, concentrated in the northern neighborhoods of Mogadishu, where residents reported artillery fire and street-to-street combat that forced thousands to flee their homes.

## Mounting Casualties

Medical staff at Madina Hospital said they had been overwhelmed by the influx of wounded, many of them civilians caught in the crossfire.

"We are receiving patients faster than we can treat them," said Dr. Amina Hassan, a physician at the facility. "Many are women and children with shrapnel injuries. Our supplies are running critically low."

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) confirmed the strain on medical facilities. "The humanitarian situation is deteriorating rapidly," an ICRC spokesperson said in a statement. "We are calling on all parties to respect international humanitarian law and to allow safe passage for the wounded and for aid workers seeking to reach those in need."

Doctors Without Borders (Médecins Sans Frontières) echoed those concerns, warning that continued fighting was cutting off access to affected areas. "Civilians must be protected, and health facilities must never be targeted," the organization said. "We urge combatants to guarantee unimpeded humanitarian access to save lives."

## The Role of Sharia Law

At the heart of the conflict lies a dispute over governance and the implementation of sharia, or Islamic law. Militant groups have long sought to impose a strict interpretation of Islamic law across the territories they control, positioning themselves in opposition to the internationally backed federal government.

The government has said it supports a moderate application of Islamic principles within a constitutional framework, while accusing the militants of using religion to justify violence and consolidate power. Analysts note that the ideological divide over the scope of sharia continues to fuel recruitment and complicate reconciliation efforts.

## Government Response

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Somali government condemned the attacks and vowed to restore order. "Our security forces are working to protect the population and defend the institutions of the state," the spokesperson said. "These groups seek to destabilize our nation, but they will not succeed."

The government urged residents to remain calm and pledged to open humanitarian corridors to allow civilians to reach safety.

## International Reaction

The U.S. Embassy for Somalia issued a statement expressing concern over the escalation. "We condemn the violence in Mogadishu and mourn the loss of innocent lives," the statement read. "The United States stands with the Somali people and supports efforts to achieve lasting peace and stability. We call on all parties to protect civilians and uphold their humanitarian obligations."

The embassy also reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Somali-led security and governance initiatives.

## An Uncertain Outlook

As of Monday, sporadic gunfire could still be heard in parts of the capital, and aid agencies warned that the number of displaced could climb into the tens of thousands if fighting continues.

For now, residents like Fatima Abdi, who fled her home with her four children, are left to wait. "We just want peace," she said from a makeshift shelter on the city's outskirts. "We have lived with war for too long."

"The claims of the apostate government are false," said Sheikh Abdiasis Abu Musab, a spokesman for the group's military operations, in a statement. "Our fighters remain in their positions and have inflicted heavy losses on the enemy. We will continue our resistance."

Humanitarian organizations warned of a deepening crisis for civilians caught in the crossfire.

"We are seeing a rapidly worsening situation," said a spokeswoman for a coalition of aid agencies operating in the region. "Thousands of families have been displaced, hospitals are overwhelmed, and there are severe shortages of clean water, food and medical supplies. Civilians are bearing the brunt of this violence."

Aid workers estimated that tens of thousands of people had been affected by the fighting, with many sheltering in makeshift camps on the city's outskirts. Medical facilities reported treating scores of wounded, including women and children.

Relief groups called on all parties to allow safe passage for civilians and unhindered access for humanitarian workers.

"We urgently need guarantees of safe corridors," the aid spokeswoman added. "People are trapped, and every hour of delay costs lives."

The current round of violence marks one of the most intense periods of urban combat in Mogadishu in recent months. Al-Shabaab, which controls swaths of territory in southern and central Somalia, has repeatedly targeted the capital with insurgent attacks despite being pushed from the city center years ago.

Government officials have vowed to press their offensive, while regional and international partners have called for restraint and the protection of civilian lives.

Fighting continued into Thursday evening, residents said, with the sound of gunfire and explosions echoing across the northern part of the city.

# Escalating Conflict in Somalia Displaces Thousands as Humanitarian Crisis Deepens

*International Desk*

MOGADISHU — Fighting between government forces and armed insurgents has intensified across several regions of Somalia in recent weeks, leaving scores dead, forcing thousands of families from their homes, and straining an already fragile humanitarian system, according to local officials and aid organizations.

## Mounting Casualties

Regional authorities reported that clashes in central and southern Somalia have resulted in significant casualties among combatants and civilians alike. Hospital officials in affected areas described treating patients with injuries consistent with mortar fire and small-arms combat, though independent verification of exact figures remains difficult due to restricted access to conflict zones.

"We are seeing the human cost of this violence every day," said one medical coordinator working in the region, who requested anonymity for security reasons. "Families are caught between the fighting with nowhere safe to go."

Casualty counts vary between sources, and both government and insurgent representatives have offered differing accounts of the toll.

## Displacement Crisis

Humanitarian agencies estimate that the recent surge in fighting has displaced thousands of people, many of whom have fled with few possessions toward makeshift settlements on the outskirts of larger towns. Aid workers warn that displacement camps are becoming overcrowded, with shortages of clean water, food, and shelter.

The new wave of displacement compounds Somalia's long-standing humanitarian challenges, where recurrent drought and instability have already uprooted large segments of the population over the past several years.

## Health Services Under Strain

Among the most acute consequences has been the disruption of medical care. Several health clinics in contested areas have suspended operations, citing safety concerns for staff and damage to facilities. The closures have left communities without access to basic treatment, maternal care, and vaccination services.

International medical charities operating in Somalia have called for the protection of health infrastructure and safe passage for medical personnel, noting that attacks on or near clinics violate humanitarian principles.

## Government Warnings

Senior government ministers have issued strong warnings to the insurgent group, vowing to restore security and hold those responsible for the violence accountable.

In public statements, government officials called on the rebels to cease hostilities and warned that security operations would continue until stability was reestablished in affected regions. Ministers also urged civilians to avoid areas of active fighting and appealed to the international community for continued support.

The insurgent group has historically rejected government authority and has continued to challenge state control across parts of the country.

## International Response

Regional bodies and international partners have expressed concern over the deteriorating situation, calling for restraint, the protection of civilians, and unhindered humanitarian access. Aid organizations have appealed for additional funding to meet the growing needs of displaced families.

Observers caution that without a durable political resolution, cycles of violence and displacement are likely to persist, deepening the suffering of ordinary Somalis caught in the crossfire.

---

*This report is a general composition. Readers seeking current, verified developments should consult established news agencies and humanitarian organizations for the latest information.*
